q: How does a hash map find a value without looking at every item?
options: A hash function turns the key into a bucket number and it jumps to that bucket
It sorts the keys and does a binary search
It keeps the keys in a linked list
It reads the items in the order they were added
why: The key becomes a number, the number picks the bucket, and we look only inside that bucket. That is O(1) on average.

options: Two equal keys are stored twice
Two different keys land in the same bucket
The table is full
A key is deleted by mistake
why: It is normal. The bucket keeps both keys in a short list and checks them until the key matches. Many collisions make lookups slow.

q: When can a hash map lookup become O(n)?
options: When the keys are numbers
When the map has more than 10 keys
When most keys land in the same bucket
Every time you call `has`
why: If every key lands in one bucket, that bucket is a long list and we walk all of it. A good hash and a table that grows keep buckets short.

options: `||` does not work with strings
Object keys cannot contain letters only
`constructor` is a reserved word that throws
`counts.constructor` already exists on a plain object (it is a function)
why: The prototype names are already there, so you add 1 to a function and get a string. A `Map` has no such trap.

q: In Two Sum with a Map, why do we store `nums[i]` AFTER checking for `target - nums[i]`?
options: So a number cannot be paired with itself
To make the Map smaller
Because `Map.set` is slow
To keep the numbers sorted
why: Checking first means we only match against numbers that came earlier. With target 10, a lone 5 must not pair with itself.
The same number twice is one member. The number 1 and the string '1' are different values.
